Stepped supply, export and import curves

Source: R/class-supply.R
supply-curve.Rd

Turn a single-price supply, export or import object into a stepped price curve: parallel steps, each with its own share of the quantity and its own price.

Usage

asSupplyCurve(
  object,
  range = NULL,
  nsteps = NULL,
  shares = NULL,
  price = NULL,
  labels = NULL,
  desc = NULL
)

asImportCurve(
  object,
  range = NULL,
  nsteps = NULL,
  shares = NULL,
  price = NULL,
  labels = NULL,
  desc = NULL
)

asExportCurve(
  object,
  range = NULL,
  nsteps = NULL,
  shares = NULL,
  price = NULL,
  labels = NULL,
  desc = NULL
)

Arguments

object

a supply, export or import object.

range

numeric of length 2, the first and last price of a linear curve.

nsteps

integer, the number of steps. Ignored when shares is given.

shares

numeric, each step's fraction of the quantity. Must be positive and sum to 1. Default equal.

price

numeric, explicit per-step prices, as an alternative to range.

labels

character, step names. Default S1, S2, ...

desc

character, per-step descriptions.

Value

An object of the same class, carrying a cluster axis.

Details

range describes a continuous linear marginal-price curve and each step is priced at the MIDPOINT of its band, which reproduces the area under that curve exactly – the quantity-weighted mean of the step prices is mean(range). Pass an explicit price vector instead for a curve that is not linear.

The steps become cluster variants, so one object expands into one ordinary object per step before interpolation and they all sum into the same commodity balance. No new variable, equation or solver-template change is involved.

Direction matters and is enforced. asSupplyCurve() and asImportCurve() require a non-decreasing curve, asExportCurve() a non-increasing one. This is not style: the solver fills the cheapest step first (or, for export, the best-paid first, since export revenue is a negative cost), and a curve running the other way is not convex.

Every finite quantity bound the object carries is split across the steps – ava.* / exp.* / imp.* and the cumulative @reserve. An object with no finite bound is refused, because an unbounded curve is meaningless.

See also

newSupply(), newExport(), newImport(), lossTranches()

Examples

SUP <- newSupply("COA", commodity = "COA",
                 supply = data.frame(ava.up = 100))
SUP <- asSupplyCurve(SUP, range = c(10, 50), nsteps = 5)
SUP@cluster
#>   cluster                                   desc order
#> 1      S1   step 1 of 5: 0-0.2 of quantity at 14     1
#> 2      S2 step 2 of 5: 0.2-0.4 of quantity at 22     2
#> 3      S3 step 3 of 5: 0.4-0.6 of quantity at 30     3
#> 4      S4 step 4 of 5: 0.6-0.8 of quantity at 38     4
#> 5      S5   step 5 of 5: 0.8-1 of quantity at 46     5
